reading.title: Putting a Broken Pot Back Together
reading.purpose: Find out how a museum expert repairs a clay pot that broke into many pieces.
paras: When a clay pot cracks into many pieces, it may look like the end of the pot. But in a museum workshop, a repair expert called a conservator sees it differently. The job is to put the pot back together. Then people can learn from it.

First, the expert lays out every piece on a table. Some pieces look unusual, with strange curves or bright colors. A few look unfamiliar because they come from a part of the pot nobody has seen. A beginner might feel uneasy, worried that the job is too big. It is unlikely that two edges will match by luck. So the expert sorts the pieces by color and thickness.

Next, she tries to rearrange the pieces until their edges line up. If a piece will not fit, she will reconsider and think again about where it goes. Sometimes a missing piece may reappear later, found in a box of dirt from the dig where the pot was discovered.

When all the pieces are ready, she will reassemble the pot with a special glue that can be removed later. The people who made the pot long ago were unaware that someone would study it today. At last, the pieces that were apart for so long reunite. They are one whole pot again.
Repair takes patience, but it lets a broken pot tell its story again.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, a missing piece may "reappear." This means it may
choices: break into even more pieces when it is handled
change color after the dirt is cleaned off
fit into a different place on the pot
come into view again after being lost
qs.why: The sentence says the missing piece is later found in a box of dirt, so it shows up again.

qs.q: Which sentence tells the first thing the expert does with the pieces?
choices: First, the expert lays out every piece on a table.
Next, she tries to rearrange the pieces until their edges line up.
When all the pieces are ready, she will reassemble the pot with a special glue that can be removed later.
Repair takes patience, but it lets a broken pot tell its story again.
qs.why: The word First marks the first step, and the sentence says she lays out every piece.

ev.text: First, the expert lays out every piece on a table.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: A broken pot is not worth saving because the job is far too hard for anyone.
Conservators work faster than anyone else who has a job inside a museum.
An expert repairs a broken pot with patience, step by step.
Most clay pots break because people dig them up and carry them to a museum.
qs.why: The reading follows the repair from laying out pieces to gluing them, and ends by saying repair takes patience.

qs.q: Why does the expert sort the pieces by color and thickness first?
choices: She wants to give the pieces back to the people who made the pot.
Sorting gives her a plan, because edges rarely match by luck.
She feels uneasy and wants to put the hardest pieces away.
Pieces of the same color are always from the same part of the pot.
qs.why: The reading says it is unlikely that two edges will match by luck, so sorting gives her a way to start.

clues.text: because they come from a part of the pot nobody has seen
worried that the job is too big
with strange curves or bright colors
think again about where it goes

reading.retellFrame: To fix a broken pot, the expert first ___, then ___, and finally ___.

needsReview.reason: States that conservators use a glue that can be removed later (reversible adhesive). This is a standard conservation practice, but a person should confirm the wording suits the grade.
